title: Science-Based Fitness needs a reality check.
summary: Prompted by Jeff Nippard's poll about taking advice from someone who knows everything about lifting but doesn't lift, NH argues that in physical domains knowledge means the ability to replicate, so theory cannot be separated from practice or from its author. He accuses science-based fitness of using 'the science' as unearned authority that dodges personal responsibility, citing title-swapping YouTubers and a Mike Israetel quote on failure training.
claims: To know something practical like lifting means being able to replicate it, not just explain it
A novice cannot judge whether someone knows lifting because he lacks the knowledge himself; he must rely on blind trust or external signs of authority
Coaches like Gregg Popovich have strategic rather than physical knowledge, but strategic knowledge must still be demonstrated by results
The two external signs of authority are social proof, which proves nothing, and evidence that the method works, such as being bigger or stronger
In pro bodybuilding coaching matters little: athletes switch coaches with little effect, many coach themselves, and drugs are the constant
Legendary bodybuilding and powerlifting coaches like Vince Gironda, Louie Simmons and Ed Coan all proved their knowledge with their own bodies first
Strategic knowledge usually stems from practical knowledge, but the reverse is not true
Talented athletes respond to almost any training, so their results may come despite a coach, citing Joel Seedman coaching NBA players
You cannot separate theory from practice in fitness; someone who knows but refuses to apply it is like a baker who won't bake a pie
The 'oncologist need not have cancer' argument is dishonest; you still judge an oncologist by results, by how many patients he cures
Judging someone's knowledge by their ability to replicate it is common sense, like asking the top student rather than the failing one for help
People would not follow Jeff Nippard if he were not big and strong; his success comes from looking the part and being likable, not the studies he cites
He likes and trusts Nippard, who helped him save his channel when it was deleted
Maybe 1% of viewers actually care about the studies in videos; the rest respond to size, strength and likability
'Science-based' is unearned authority that lets creators dismiss others without arguments and escape responsibility when a study is later disproven
A YouTuber renamed 'How to grow your legs with SCIENCE' to 'SCIENCE IS WRONG' without changing the content, showing the label is just marketing
In his view people are turning away from science-based content toward people with demonstrable experience; about 70% in the poll would not take advice from someone who never lifted
Real evidence-based lifting is experience-based lifting times ten, pooling many people's experience, but current science-based fitness robs people of agency
Mike Israetel's claim that people only like failure training because it's hardcore shames lifters' own conclusions and cherry-picks both studies and bodybuilders
Real science means skepticism and questioning everything; modern science-based fitness has become closer to a cult or scientism
